newsitem.title: UK: Commonwealth Nigeria team goes, key minister stays.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth Nigeria team goes, key minister stays.

text.p: A Commonwealth fact-finding team due to hold talks in Nigeria on restoring democracy suffered a blow on Monday when a key member of the group pulled out of the trip just hours before it began.

Canadian Secretary of State for Latin America and Africa, Christine Stewart, decided not to travel after the Nigerian authorities declined to issue visas to two Canadian security officers due to accompany the delegation.
The decision is embarrassing both for the Commonwealth and Canada, which has taken a consistently hard line on the Nigerian military government over its alleged human rights violations.

"The Canadian withdrawal will be a huge disappointment to the Commonwealth secretariat and other members of the mission, because without Canada they lose some of the leverage they had," said Professor James Manor, director of the Institute of Commonwealth Studies.

The Commonwealth suspended Nigeria last year after it hanged nine minority rights activists, including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa, but since then deep splits have emerged on how best to push Abuja back to democracy.

The eight-nation Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) resolved its differences in September when it decided not to impose a set of agreed sanctions on Nigeria and instead to keep the dialogue going by sending the fact-finding mission.
But it was clear that Canada, which had taken a tough stance on Abuja and unilaterally imposed the sanctions, was unhappy at being obliged to toe the line.

"It may be that the Canadians are pulling out for more than security reasons. They have been disappointed from the start by the failure of other Commonwealth nations to be as assertive as they have been," Manor said by telephone.
"Perhaps they feel the the mission will be a failure and want to cut their losses before the start."

Stewart's refusal to travel meant only seven CMAG ministers took off for talks which are likely to be difficult, especially since the rulers of the oil-rich West African nation show no signs of yielding ground on any issue.
Canadian officials in London were not available to comment on Stewart's change of mind, which appeared to be connected to the high crime levels in Nigeria.

"(Stewart's decision) is certainly very unfortunate but the fact that the group has decided to go means that it has decided it can carry out the work it was asked to do," Commonwealth spokesman Michael Fathers said by telephone.
The 53-nation Commonwealth, which mainly groups Britain and its former colonies, wants military ruler General Sani Abacha to speed up the planned transition to civilian rule.
But Lagos-based diplomats said they expected Nigeria to continue insisting that it would not start talking about democracy until the suspension had been discussed.
The Abuja meeting should have taken place months ago but it was postponed after Nigeria refused to allow CMAG to meet high profile detainees and opposition groups in the country.
CMAG is made up of foreign ministers of Britain, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Ghana, Jamaica and Malaysia.
